questions.prompt: a and b are real numbers. Which work shows that (a + bi)(a - bi) is always a real number?
questions.prompt_markup: a and b are real numbers. Which work shows that (a + bi)(a - bi) is always a real number?

choices.text: (a + bi)(a - bi) = a² - abi + abi - b²i² = a² - b²(-1) = a² + b², which is real.
(a + bi)(a - bi) = a² - b², which is real.
(3 + 2i)(3 - 2i) = 13 is real, so every such product is real.
(a + bi)(a - bi) = a² - b²i², and a² - b²i² is real because it has no i in it.

questions.correct_answer: (a + bi)(a - bi) = a² - abi + abi - b²i² = a² - b²(-1) = a² + b², which is real.
questions.grading_note: The middle terms cancel and i² = -1. The others treat i² as having no i (without simplifying), lose the sign from i² = -1, or check one example.

questions.standard_level: Algebra II. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Algebra II, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: c and d are real and not both 0. Why does multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator c + di always give a real denominator?
questions.prompt_markup: c and d are real and not both 0. Why does multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator c + di always give a real denominator?

choices.text: (c + di)(c - di) = c² - d², a real number (the middle terms cancel).
The conjugate c - di is itself a real number, so any product with it is real.
Multiplying by any complex number makes the denominator real.
(c + di)(c - di) = c² + d², a real number (positive because c and d are not both 0).

questions.correct_answer: (c + di)(c - di) = c² + d², a real number (positive because c and d are not both 0).
questions.grading_note: The product of a number and its conjugate is c² + d². The others lose the sign from i² = -1, call c - di real, or overgeneralize ((1 + i)(1 + i) = 2i).
